The report highlights the risks posed to federal information systems by the global IT supply chain. These risks include the potential for security vulnerabilities in hardware and software components, as well as the possibility of unauthorized access or data breaches during the manufacturing and distribution process. However, there is still work to be done to fully address these risks, particularly in ensuring the effective implementation and enforcement of supply chain protection measures.

The report recommends that federal agencies develop and document departmental policies for protecting against supply chain threats, as well as procedures for implementing and monitoring these protections. It also recommends that agencies verify compliance with these measures and assess their effectiveness on an ongoing basis.

The report concludes by emphasizing the importance of addressing IT supply chain risks in order to protect federal information systems and safeguard against potential security breaches or data losses. The report examines the compliance of the Departments of Labor (DOL), Health and Human Services (HHS), and Justice (DOJ) with statutory restrictions on religious discrimination in grant awards between 2007 and 2015. The report found that DOL identified 117 grantees potentially exempt from religious discrimination restrictions, of which 6 were not contacted to confirm their eligibility. DOJ identified 66 grantees, of which 9 were not contacted. HHS identified one grant program, the Poverty and Homelessness Prevention and Rapid Re-housing Program, which had not been reviewed for compliance with religious discrimination restrictions since 2007. The report also found that all three departments provided information on religious discrimination restrictions to grantees, but the methods of communication varied. DOL and DOJ required grantees to self-certify their eligibility for exemptions, while HHS required grantees to submit a self-certification and undergo a review process. The report recommends that all three departments improve their processes for ensuring compliance with religious discrimination restrictions, including regular reviews of grant programs and clearer communication with grantees. The report was shared with the relevant departments and will be made available to the public.

The report examines the use of Electronic Advance Data (EAD) by the United States Postal Service (USPS) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to target mail for inspection. The report recommends that USPS and CBP establish performance goals for the pilots, collect data on their effectiveness, and assess the costs and benefits of using EAD compared to other methods of mail selection for inspection. The Department of Homeland Security concurred with the recommendations. The report also mentions that USPS has faced financial challenges in recent years, adding to the importance of carefully considering the costs and benefits of using EAD for mail selection for inspection.

The report examines the compliance of the Departments of Labor (DOL), Justice (DOJ), and Health and Human Services (HHS) with statutory restrictions on religious-based hiring in grants awarded between 2007 and 2015. DOL and DOJ grantees were required to self-certify their eligibility for an exemption, which was then reviewed by the agencies. DOL implemented a more stringent review process, requiring grantees to submit their request for exemption to the agency for approval. DOL also implemented a 30-day turnaround time for reviewing and responding to exemption requests.

The report identified nine faith-based grantees that received exemptions from statutory restrictions on religious-based hiring between 2007 and 2015. These grantees were primarily focused on providing services related to sexual assault, domestic violence, and human trafficking. The grantees argued that their religious beliefs were central to their mission and that hiring staff who shared those beliefs was essential to effectively delivering services.

The report also found that five faith-based grantees that did not request exemptions were unaware of the availability of such exemptions. The agencies were criticized for not adequately communicating the availability and process for requesting exemptions to grantees.

The report recommends that the agencies improve their communication with grantees regarding the availability and process for requesting exemptions from statutory restrictions on religious-based hiring. The report also suggests that the agencies consider providing more guidance and clarity on the criteria for granting exemptions.
